This posts rightly highlights an important area of evolution in hiring practices today. Truly hands-on, multidisciplinary profiles take time to develop, which naturally happens when individuals are given the right opportunities to grow.

Keyword-based matching and niche skill-set hiring can sometimes make the market a bit challenging to navigate. While a wonderful balance is on-the-job learning, the rapid pace of skill evolution means organizations are constantly finding new ways to stay flexible and agile.

When companies focus on maximizing current expertise, it often sparks a healthy internal conversation around how to continuously support employee growth and retention. 

Market is experimenting with different models to meet these unique needs.

For instance, contract hiring provides a helpful pathway—offering full-time, focused engagements that serve specific requirements and project timelines very well, even if they come with natural project cycles.

We also see various collaborative approaches, such as consulting companies partnering with other companies to source specialized, project-based talent on the payroll of sourcing company. 

Similarly, global AI research initiatives often connect host locations with regional talent hubs to engage freelancers flexibly, without demanding restrictive exclusivity or rigid full-time commitments.

These multi-layered approaches bring wonderful flexibility to the ecosystem. At the same time, it is always inspiring to look at how ground realities can be optimized to ensure all participants thrive.

The exciting implication here is an opportunity for the market: companies can directly partner with specialized consulting firms that are truly multidisciplinary in nature on project basis. This direct collaboration can create a streamlined, positive experience for everyone—helping organizations access integrated expertise smoothly while empowering talent with meaningful, well-supported engagements.

I think I could write more, but maybe I should stop here for now. I'd like to hear your thoughts!

Rejected for a job, a loan or a phone contract, and no human ever looked at your file?

The GDPR gives you the right to know that an automated decision was made about you, and to receive meaningful information about the logic behind it (Art. 22, read with Art. 13(2)(f), 14(2)(g) and 15(1)(h)).

But how far does this right really go, now that AI is moving into hiring, credit scoring, pricing and fraud detection? The models are complex, often provided by third parties, and protected as trade secrets.

The CJEU gave a clear response in Dun & Bradstreet Austria (C-203/22, February 2025).

A consumer was refused a mobile phone contract after an automated credit assessment and asked how the system reached that result.

The Court held:
The company must explain, in clear and plain language, the procedure and principles actually applied to that person's data. It does not have to disclose the full algorithm or source code, but it must give enough to let the person understand and contest the decision.

Trade secrets are not a blanket excuse: where protected information is involved, a court or supervisory authority must balance the protection of that information against the person's right of access.

Therefore, decisions made by AI that affect people's rights or opportunities cannot stay a black box. So when companies ask themselves "can we automate this?", they should also ask "can we explain this?"

And increasingly, that is no longer just a question of good governance - it can be a question of legal compliance.

Before You Invest in AI Everywhere, Start with Compliance.

One of the most common lawsuits a business will face isn't a product issue, contract dispute, or cybersecurity event. It's an employment-related claim.
As organizations grow across states, cities, and counties, keeping up with constantly changing employment laws becomes incredibly challenging. 

That’s why I enjoyed listening to the latest At Work in America podcast featuring Steve Boese, Trish Steed, and Kimball Dean Parker, CEO of SixFifty.

A few key takeaways:
- Employment compliance is becoming more complex than ever, especially for multi-state employers.
- AI can help automate highly repetitive compliance tasks such as employee handbooks, policy updates, required notices, and hiring documentation.
- The best results come from combining AI with proven legal frameworks and workflows, not simply asking generative AI to provide an answer.
- Strong compliance infrastructure does more than reduce risk. It enables growth, supports hiring in new markets, and frees HR teams to focus on people and strategy.

I particularly liked Kimball's perspective that compliance may be one of the most practical and immediate use cases for AI in HR. When technology can remove administrative burden while improving confidence in compliance decisions, everyone wins.

For HR leaders, compliance isn't just a legal requirement. It's a business enabler.

Who is liable and accountable for AI's use in hiring? 

For the first time, liability for AI’s use in hiring is being laid at the door of the developer of technology (the vendor) rather than a deployer (the employer) in two landmark legal cases (Mobley v Workday and Kistler et al v Eightfold). 

Court timelines move slowly – these two suits wont be resolved for months, if not years. But no organization that builds, sells or uses AI in hiring can afford to wait for a verdict before acting.

For reporting in UNLEASH, I spoke to Heather Bussing from Bussing Law, Jason M. Loring, FIP, CIPP/US, CIPM at Jones Walker LLP & Kyle Lagunas from Kyle & Co about what HR buyer need to know (and do) now. I also spoke to the vendors themselves on these suits. 

Spoiler, building not buying is not the answer. Vendors will always be important partners; there is just a need to think carefully about the boundaries, the contracts and the documentation.

Would you lend $100 million against a GPU?

The AI boom is creating a new question for credit markets.

As billions flow into data centres and computing infrastructure, lenders increasingly have to decide what they are actually underwriting:

the hardware — or the cash flow behind it?

A cutting-edge GPU may be extremely valuable today. But technology moves quickly. A new generation of chips can arrive long before a five-year loan reaches maturity.

That creates a difficult credit question:

If the asset securing your loan loses value faster than expected, what protects the lender?

For me, the stronger starting point would be contracted cash flow from a financially strong customer rather than relying primarily on the residual value of the hardware.

But even that would not be enough on its own.

I would still want to understand:

• Who is the counterparty?
• How long is the revenue contracted?
• Can cash flow comfortably service the debt?
• What happens if construction or deployment is delayed?
• What covenants protect the lender if performance deteriorates?

This is what makes the AI investment cycle interesting from a finance perspective.

The conversation is no longer only:

“Which AI company will win?”

It is increasingly:

“Who finances the buildout, what supports the debt, and who absorbs the downside if expectations change?”

Now I want to hear from people working in banking, credit and investments:

Which would you rather lend against?

A — $100M of advanced GPU hardware
B — A long-term contract with an investment-grade customer

And more importantly:

What is the ONE covenant you would insist on before approving the loan?

I’m genuinely interested to see whether bankers, investors and students answer this differently.

The employee experiences one problem.

HR experiences several queues, systems, teams & policies.

That is where hidden administration accumulates. 

In my experience, the most time consuming HR process sits underneath recruitment, onboarding and payroll. 

It is the employee and manager HR service resolution. 

It is the constant flow of questions, manager requests, payroll corrections, policy interpretation, approval chasing, system updates, data fixes and escalations.

I lived this in every single one of my HR roles and today I see them in my client's HR function. 

A good HR process is a connected service that turns a real employee or business need into a reliable outcome. 

A process map that begins at Step 1 and ends at Step 8 is incomplete. 

Map this instead:

Input → Activity → Decision → Output → Outcome

Let's take an example of a request to change working pattern:

1. Inputs →
Employee ID, current contract, proposed hours, effective date, manager rationale and policy criteria.

2. Activities →
Capture the request, check it, review it with the manager, assess it against policy, update the contract and HRIS, notify payroll and confirm to the employee.

3. Decision →
Approve or decline, and who has the authority to do it.

4. Outputs →
A documented decision, an updated contract and employee record, a payroll instruction and a written confirmation.

5. Outcome →
A fair, timely decision, with records and pay that match what was agreed.

Then ask who owns each important data element and which system is authoritative. 

Ask whether each decision is necessary, rules-based or judgement-based, and who has authority.

Do not automate a decision because a system can make it, especially where it affects hiring, pay, performance, discipline or redundancy.

The sequence is: Eliminate → Simplify → Standardise → Digitise → Automate → AI-assist

A good HR process is clear enough to own, simple enough to run, reliable enough to trust and safe enough to scale.

🔻 Sectors Feeling the Squeeze: High-leverage discretionary tech, speculative Web3/crypto platforms, and third-party IT service aggregators. 🛡️ Hotspots Hiring Heavy: BFSI/FinTech (Risk & Quantitative Analytics), Healthcare/Pharma (Clinical Data & Compliance), and Enterprise SaaS/Retail Tech.

3. What GCCs Demand from Data & Business Analysts Right Now:
❌ What won't get you hired: Just pulling raw SQL tables or building 15 static, un-governed Power BI dashboards.

💡 Bottom Line: When markets wobble globally, product MNCs don't stop spending—they redirect capital to high-value GCC capability hubs. If you are positioning yourself as an AI-Governed Data/Business Analyst, Q4 is your biggest opportunity.

How to get out of client delivery so your agency can grow past $40k a month:

(This is the stage mapping I run with agencies at Systemised, and it's the first thing I'd fix before hiring anyone.)

First of all...

If you're doing $10k to $40k a month and you're still in every client thread, your own time is now the ceiling.

- You check every deliverable before it goes out
- Clients message you directly, even with a team in place
- Onboarding waits until you have a free afternoon
- Nobody else knows what "done" looks like

That works at five clients. At fifteen it eats the hours you should be spending on sales.

So this is the order I'd take you out of it:

1. Write out every stage a client goes through

From signed contract to renewal. For example: contract signed, onboarding form in, kickoff call, first deliverable, weekly update, monthly review, renewal.

If you can't list it in one sitting, that's the first problem, because it only exists in your head.

2. Put a name next to every stage

Go down the list and write who does it today. At this stage it's usually your name on most of them.

3. Delete, automate, then delegate

Delete the stages that only exist out of habit. Automate the admin, like the onboarding form, folder setup, kickoff booking and update reminders. Then delegate what's left, apart from the few moments that need your judgment.

4. Define done for every stage you hand over

Bad: "Send the client their monthly report."

Good: "Report goes out by the 3rd. It covers leads, booked calls and cost per booked call against last month, plus one recommendation. The account manager sends it and only flags it to the founder if a number got worse."

Someone in their first week can run the second one.

5. Move client comms off your phone

Give every client one shared channel with a named owner who replies. You only step in when that owner escalates something.

6. Keep your human stages on purpose

Strategy calls, big renewals and the moment a client is unhappy stay with you, because that's where your judgment is worth the most.

Do this before you hire. A new hire dropped into delivery that was never mapped just becomes another person asking you questions.

A founder-independent agency starts with a written list of stages and a name next to each one.

Hiring and AI only help once that list exists.

Something I’ve noticed recently… 🤓🤖


AI is becoming a much bigger part of banking hiring.. 

I’ve been speaking to quite a few people in the market and the interesting thing is, it’s not all about hiring AI developers.

A lot of the demand is for people who already know banking risk, compliance, data, trading, cyber, payments etc but also have a good understanding of AI and how it can actually be used.

Which makes sense really.. Banks can’t just throw something into production and hope for the best 😂 There’s regulation, security, governance, risk… and about 100 other things to think about.

So I think people who understand the tech + the banking side are going to be in a really good position.

Definitely seeing more conversations around AI, Python, data and automation at the moment, particularly across contract and consulting work.

Interested to know what other people are seeing though… Are you seeing more AI roles coming through in banking, or are things still pretty cautious?

I read a long piece on AI automation this week and one idea stuck with me: automate the whole workflow, not the single task.
"Draft an email" is a task. Receiving a lead, checking whether it fits, researching the company, drafting a reply, logging it and scheduling the follow-up is a workflow. That's where the time actually goes.
The author suggests treating an AI agent like a junior colleague: a narrow job description, limited access, a review step, and a record of what it did. Anything involving contracts, payments or hiring stays with a human.
The 30-day plan is simple. Week one, find the repetitive work. Week two, build one small prototype. Week three, test it on real cases. Then decide whether it earned the right to expand.
I'd add one thing: measure outcomes like response time and error rate, not how many things the automation produced.
What's the one weekly bottleneck you would hand off first?

I hope this post is received in the way it’s intended. As advice and encouragement, especially for anyone having a tough time finding work.

With AI, inflation, cutbacks, layoffs, and bias in hiring, there are talented people on here describing hundreds, sometimes thousands, of applications with little or no response.

👎Tailoring every CV.
👎Reaching out directly.
👎Following advice.
👎Trying a different approach.
👎Still getting nowhere.

At what point do you say, “I need to pivot”?

I don’t think there’s a fixed number of weeks or applications. Your finances, responsibilities, and the market you’re targeting all matter.

But you don’t have to wait until you’ve exhausted yourself or your savings to explore a different route.

If several weeks of focused effort aren’t generating conversations, take stock. Speak to people who know your market and will give you an honest view.

Is the issue how you’re presenting your experience? 
The roles you’re targeting? 
Or has demand for that work changed?

Those are different problems, and each needs a different response.

A pivot could mean taking your skills into another industry, considering an adjacent role, widening your search, or doing contract work while you work out the next step.

It doesn’t have to mean starting again.

I think we’re going through a significant shift in how people find work and how businesses bring talent in. That creates uncertainty, but it also opens up possibilities.

AI tools and learning platforms make it easier to learn, test an idea, and build something with a small team or limited capital.  That won’t be the right route for everyone. 

When you need an income, “go and build something” can sound painfully detached from reality.

But if you have some room, start small. Solve a problem you understand. Test whether someone will pay for your help. Give yourself another option alongside the job search.

You don’t need to abandon your experience. You may need to find a different place to apply it.

And needing to change direction isn’t a reflection of your worth. 🙏

A supplier can become very good at doing work that its client is gradually forgetting how to do. That may be acceptable when outsourcing is a deliberate permanent choice. It becomes more troubling when temporary support quietly becomes the operating model.

I ran an embedded talent company before the model became fashionable. We helped clients when building a permanent recruitment team didn’t make sense, but our aim was always to leave them better able to hire without us. External support should build capability as well as provide capacity.

The supplier learns through every cycle while knowledge inside the client can disappear. Mariana Mazzucato describes a similar effect as institutional infantilisation: prolonged outsourcing can leave an organisation progressively less able to operate without external support. The client pays for the learning but may retain very little of it.

An RPO brought in for a hiring surge provides flexible capacity. If it remains embedded for years, recruitment has become an ongoing requirement while the capability remains external. Budget treatment may encourage this: an internal team appears as headcount, while an RPO can sit within procurement spend. Both are operating costs, but the latter can sit outside the headcount budget and be presented as variable capacity.

That flexibility also shifts responsibility for downsizing to the supplier. The client reduces its requirement; the RPO manages the staffing consequences, and its recruiters may bear the insecurity. Where redeployment isn’t possible, costs can extend to households and public support. The client’s savings don’t capture all the consequences of its decision. Who pays belongs alongside what it saves.

Internal leadership changes too. Building capability, developing people and improving decisions can give way to selecting suppliers, monitoring service levels and managing contracts. The leader remains accountable for the outcome while owning progressively less of what is needed to produce it.

This may help explain the insecurity felt by many TA leaders. It isn’t simply the arrival of AI. Volatility encouraged organisations to rent recruitment capacity, making internal teams easier to reduce. As internal knowledge disappeared, dependence on external provision grew and leadership became more precarious. An RPO doesn’t inflict this upon an organisation; it happens when outsourcing is used without a strategy for what should remain inside.

When the supplier leaves, is the organisation better able to perform the work—or merely looking for its next supplier?
